analogy.p: A **client-server** network is like a school canteen: the pupils (clients) queue and ask for what they want, the canteen staff (the server) prepare it, check who is allowed what (free school meals, allergies) and hand it over. Everything is organised, controlled and fairly safe, but if the canteen closes nobody gets lunch and it costs a lot to run. A **peer-to-peer** network is like friends having a picnic where everyone brings their own food and shares it directly: it costs almost nothing and nobody is in charge, but nobody is keeping check on what is shared, there is no spare food if someone doesn't turn up and the picnic stops working well if too many people arrive. The analogy breaks down because in a computer network a server can serve thousands of clients at once at great speed, and in P2P file sharing more peers can actually make downloading faster, which a picnic cannot do.
analogy.t: The school canteen and the picnic

bullets: Describe the **client-server** model: clients request services, servers provide them and manage the network.
Describe the **peer-to-peer** model: devices are equal, each stores its own files and can share them directly, with no central server.
Give **advantages and disadvantages** of each, covering cost, security, backup, reliability, management and performance.
Give **examples** of each (a school or company network and web browsing for client-server; small home networks and file sharing for P2P).
Choose and **justify** the most suitable model for a given scenario using the features of the scenario.
Understand that both models run over a **LAN or WAN** and are about roles of devices, not size of area.
core.h: What the specification asks you to know
core.p: OCR J277 section 1.3 requires you to understand the **client-server** and **peer-to-peer (P2P)** models of networking. You must be able to describe how each one works, who does what, and to give the **advantages and disadvantages** of each so that you can recommend and justify the better model for a given situation. The key idea is where the **resources and control** live: in client-server they are centralised on one or more powerful servers, whereas in peer-to-peer every device is equal and shares directly with the others. The topic is tested as 1 to 2 mark definitions, 3 to 4 mark compare questions and 6 mark scenario questions where you recommend a model for a school, a business or a home.

bullets: The model describes the **roles** of devices, not the physical layout; the same cables could support either model.
Both models can be used on a **LAN** or a **WAN**, for example the Internet uses client-server for the web and peer-to-peer for some file-sharing.
In client-server the roles are **fixed** (a device is a client or a server); in P2P each device **plays both roles**.
The bigger and more important the network, the more likely an organisation will choose **client-server** for control and security.
Many real networks are **hybrids**, but in the exam treat them as two separate models.
Remember the one-line summaries: client-server = **centralised**; peer-to-peer = **decentralised**.
core.h: Two ways to organise a network
core.p: A network is not only cables and hardware: it also has a **logical organisation** that decides which devices provide services and which ones use them. There are two models you must know. In a **client-server network** some devices are dedicated **servers** that provide resources and services, and the other devices are **clients** that ask for them. In a **peer-to-peer network** there is **no dedicated server**: every device, called a **peer**, has equal status and can both use and provide resources. Choosing between them is a trade-off between **control, security and reliability** on one side and **cost and simplicity** on the other.

bullets: **Step 1**: the client sends a **request** (for example 'open this file' or 'show this web page').
**Step 2**: the server checks who is asking, for example it **authenticates** the user with a username and password and checks their access rights.
**Step 3**: the server finds or creates the data or runs the program needed.
**Step 4**: the server sends a **response** back to that client only.
**Step 5**: the client displays or uses the result; a single server handles many such requests from many clients at once.
Clients usually **do not talk to each other directly**; communication goes through the server.
core.p: In the **client-server** model a **client** is a device (or program such as a web browser) that **requests** a service, and a **server** is a powerful computer that is always on and **provides** the service by responding to those requests. When you open a web page, your browser (the client) sends a request to a web server, the server finds the page and sends it back as a response, and your browser displays it. This is called the **request-response** cycle. The server is the **central point** of the network, so it also stores the shared files, holds the user accounts and decides who is allowed to access what.

bullets: **File server**: stores users' files centrally so they can be accessed from any computer and backed up from one place.
**Web server**: stores web pages and sends them to browsers that request them.
**Email server**: sends, receives and stores email for users.
**Print server**: manages a queue of print jobs sent to shared printers.
**Database server**: stores and answers queries on a database (for example the school's records).
**Authentication server**: checks usernames and passwords before allowing access and applies permissions.
core.p: A server is defined by its **job**, not by the shape of the computer: a server could be a rack-mounted machine in a cupboard or a virtual machine in the cloud. Large organisations often use several servers, each dedicated to one type of service, which spreads the work and means one fault does not stop everything. The server computers normally have **faster processors, more memory, larger and more reliable storage** and a connection that is always on, because many clients depend on them.

bullets: **Centralised backup**: all files are stored on the server, so one automatic backup protects everything and data is recoverable if a client breaks.
**Better security**: the administrator sets **user accounts, passwords, permissions** and installs security software in one place, so users can only see what they are allowed to see.
**Easier management**: software updates, new accounts and settings are applied centrally rather than machine by machine.
**Shared resources**: files, printers and internet access are shared, and the same file can be used from any client.
**Reliable and powerful**: servers are built for continuous use, often with backup power and duplicate (redundant) hardware.
**Scalable**: more clients can be added and the server upgraded to cope.
core.p: The strength of client-server is **centralisation**. Because the important data and the control sit in one place, an administrator can manage the whole network efficiently and keep it secure, and users get a consistent experience wherever they log in. This is why schools, businesses, banks and hospitals use it. The model is also **scalable**: if more users join, you can upgrade the server or add more servers rather than replacing every machine.

bullets: **Single point of failure**: if the server goes down, clients lose access to shared files and services.
**Expensive**: servers, server operating systems, backup systems and skilled staff all cost money.
**Needs expert administration**: someone must configure, maintain and secure the server.
**Overloading**: if too many clients make requests at once the server slows down or becomes unavailable; the more clients, the more load on the server.
**Target for attack**: because all data is in one place a successful hacker, or a denial of service attack, can have a big impact.
**Network dependent**: clients can usually do little useful work with shared data if the connection to the server is lost.
core.p: The main weakness of client-server is **dependence on the server**. All clients rely on it, so if it fails, is overloaded or is attacked, the whole network (or the service it provides) can stop. It also costs more to set up and run, because it needs specialist hardware, server software licences and a **network manager** who knows what they are doing. Finally, performance is shared: when too many clients send requests at the same time the server can become a **bottleneck** and everyone's response slows down.

bullets: Each device is **both a client and a server** depending on what it is doing at that moment.
Files are stored on the **individual devices**, not in one central place.
Devices connect **directly** to each other, often through a simple switch or wireless router.
There is **no dedicated network administrator**; each user looks after their own computer and sharing settings.
Typically used on **small networks** such as a home or a very small office with a few computers.
On the Internet, **file-sharing** (such as BitTorrent) is a well-known P2P system: pieces of a file are downloaded from many peers at once.
core.p: In a **peer-to-peer** network every computer is a **peer**: all devices have **equal status** and there is **no central server**. Each peer **stores its own files** and can share them directly with other peers, and each can also use resources shared by the others. Any peer can therefore act as both a client (when it downloads a file) and a server (when others download from it). Because nobody is in charge, there is no central account list or central backup, and each user is responsible for their own device and what they share.

bullets: **Cheaper**: no expensive server hardware, software or full-time administrator is needed.
**Easy to set up** and maintain for a small number of devices.
**No single point of failure**: if one peer fails, the others can carry on working and sharing with each other (though the failed peer's own files are not available).
**No dependence on a server's performance**: there is no server to become overloaded, so the network is not slowed by a central bottleneck.
**In file-sharing, more peers can mean faster downloads** because the file is available from many sources at once, the opposite of a client-server where more clients slow the server.
Each user has **control over their own files** and what they share.
core.p: Peer-to-peer is attractive because it is **cheap and simple**. You do not need to buy a server or pay for a specialist administrator, and a few computers can be linked and sharing files within minutes. Because there is no server, there is also no single point whose failure can shut down the network. These advantages make P2P suitable for small networks where the data is not very sensitive.

bullets: **No central backup**: each device must be backed up separately, so data can be lost if a device fails.
**Weaker security**: no central control of passwords and permissions; each computer has its own settings and may be poorly protected.
**Harder to manage** as the network grows: there is no easy way to apply updates or settings to all computers.
**Performance of a peer drops** when other peers access its shared files while it is also being used.
**Files only available when the peer is on**: if a computer is switched off, its shared files cannot be reached.
**Risk of malware and illegal content**: files from unknown peers may contain viruses, and sharing copyright material without permission is illegal.
core.p: The same lack of central control causes the main problems with P2P. Without a server there is **no central place to back up data**, so files on each machine must be backed up separately, and if a device breaks its files can be lost. Security is also weaker because each device manages its own protection, there are no central user accounts and malware or unwanted users can spread more easily between peers. Finally, performance of an individual peer can suffer when others access its files.

bullets: **Control**: a client-server network is managed centrally by an administrator, whereas a P2P network has no central control.
**Cost**: client-server needs a server and expertise so is more expensive, whereas P2P is cheaper.
**Security**: client-server allows central permissions and security software, whereas in P2P each device is responsible for its own.
**Backup**: central backup in client-server, whereas each device is backed up separately in P2P.
**Failure**: if the server fails clients lose the service, whereas in P2P the other peers can carry on.
**Scale**: client-server suits large networks with many users, whereas P2P suits small networks with few users.
core.p: In a compare question you need to put a point about client-server alongside a point about peer-to-peer. The most useful points are **where files are stored**, **who is in control**, **cost**, **security**, **backup** and **what happens when something fails**. Use words like 'whereas' and 'however'. A well-made table in your head is: control (central versus none), cost (higher versus lower), security (stronger versus weaker), backup (central versus individual), reliability (server is a single point of failure versus no single point) and typical size (large versus small).

bullets: **School, hospital, bank, large office** (many users, confidential data, need permissions and backups) -> **client-server**.
**Home network with two or three computers sharing a printer** (few users, low cost) -> **peer-to-peer** is adequate.
**Small business with five staff sharing non-sensitive files** -> P2P might work, but if customer data is held, client-server is safer.
Large public services such as **websites, online games and streaming** use client-server so that the provider controls the content and accounts.
If asked for a **justification**, structure it: 'Recommend X because (feature) which suits (scenario fact), whereas Y would (drawback).'
Do not say one model is 'better' in general; say which is better **for this scenario** and why.
core.h: Choosing the right model for a scenario
core.p: The skill the exam tests is **applying** the features to a situation. Read the scenario for clues: the **number of users**, whether the data is **sensitive or important**, the **budget**, and whether there is **IT expertise**. If there are many users, sensitive data and a need for backups and control, client-server is the better answer. If there are just a few users, little money and no special data, peer-to-peer is suitable. Always give a **reason linked to the scenario**, not just a recommendation.

bullets: **Web browsing**: browser (client) requests a page from a web server and receives a response.
**School network**: students log in through an authentication server, save work on a file server and print through a print server.
**Email**: your email app is a client connecting to the provider's mail server.
**Online games** often connect each player (client) to a game server that controls the game world.
**Home network**: laptops and a printer on a home router sharing files directly is simple peer-to-peer sharing.
**BitTorrent-type file sharing**: a file is split into pieces and each peer downloads pieces from, and uploads pieces to, many other peers.
core.p: Examples make your answers concrete and gain marks when asked to 'give an example'. Everyday life contains plenty of both models, although you may not notice them. The **World Wide Web** is the biggest client-server system: your browser is the client and websites are held on web servers. In contrast, **BitTorrent-style file sharing** is P2P and does not rely on a central server holding the file.

bullets: Central **user accounts and permissions** are a major reason organisations choose client-server.
The server can be **monitored and logged**, helping to spot misuse or attacks.
**Software updates and security patches** can be pushed from the server to all clients.
Backups can be **automatic and scheduled** and copies can be stored in a different building in case of fire.
In P2P, security depends on each user; **one infected peer can spread malware** to the others quickly.
This links to section 1.4 on **network security**: passwords, firewalls, user access levels and encryption.
core.h: Security, backup and management in more depth
core.p: Security and management are the points where the two models differ most and these are popular 4 to 6 mark discussion areas. In client-server, the administrator creates **user accounts with usernames and passwords**, gives each group **access rights** (for example students can read but not delete shared resources), installs **antivirus and a firewall** centrally and can monitor activity. In P2P each user must manage their own sharing settings, so mistakes (such as sharing a whole drive) are easy and there is no central log. Backups follow the same pattern: a server can be backed up on a schedule to another location, whereas P2P depends on every user remembering to back up.

bullets: **LAN and WAN (previous point)**: both models operate over either type of network.
**Hardware (next points)**: switches and routers carry the requests and responses between clients, servers and peers.
**The Internet, DNS and hosting**: web hosting is a client-server arrangement.
**Cloud storage**: a client-server model where the provider's data centres are the servers.
**Network security (1.4)**: user access levels, passwords and backups are central to client-server management.
**Topologies**: star networks often have a central switch connected to a server.
core.p: Client-server and peer-to-peer connect closely with the other parts of section 1.3. The hardware you will study next (NICs, switches, routers) is what physically connects the clients, servers and peers. **Cloud computing** is an extension of client-server where the server is run by a provider over the Internet. The topic of **DNS and web hosting** is all about clients requesting pages from servers. Understanding the models also helps with questions on **performance**, because a busy server is a bottleneck, and **security**, because centralised control is easier to defend.

exam: **1 mark**: client = 'a device that requests a service from a server'; server = 'a computer that provides services/resources to clients'; peer = 'a device that can act as both client and server'.
**2 mark 'describe' questions**: give how it works and an extra detail, e.g. 'In client-server the clients send requests to a server (1), which responds and manages files and security centrally (1)'.
**3 to 4 mark compare questions**: pair points on cost, control/management, security/backup and reliability using 'whereas'. Give one example each if asked.

**6 mark scenario questions**: pick a model, give 3 or more reasons linked to the scenario, mention an advantage and a disadvantage of the other model, and conclude. Use scenario details (number of users, sensitivity of data, budget).
Use key phrases: '**central server**', '**single point of failure**', '**backed up centrally**', '**user permissions**', '**each device stores its own files**', '**no dedicated server**'.
A very common mark is '**client-server: easier to manage security and backups centrally**'; the common opposite is '**P2P: no central backup or control**'.
Always say **why**: 'it is cheaper because it does not need a server' is better than 'it is cheaper'.
Do not just define the terms when asked to 'explain': add the consequence (so, because, which means).
If asked to **evaluate** or **discuss**, mention both sides and finish with a justified decision.
Avoid vague answers such as 'it is more secure'; say 'permissions can be set centrally so users can only access files they are allowed to'.

mistakes.r: A server is a computer that **provides a service or resources to clients** and usually manages the network; explain its **role**.
mistakes.w: A server is just a big computer.

mistakes.r: P2P has **weaker security** because there is no central control of accounts and permissions; each device must protect itself.
mistakes.w: Peer-to-peer has no security at all.

mistakes.r: Choose according to the **scenario**: client-server for many users and sensitive data, P2P for a small cheap network.
Clients send requests **to the server**, which responds; they do not normally communicate directly.
mistakes.w: In client-server the clients talk directly to each other.

mistakes.r: There is **no server**: each peer **stores its own files** and shares them directly.
mistakes.w: In peer-to-peer the files are on the server.

mistakes.r: The other peers can **carry on**; only the failed peer's files are unavailable. It is client-server that has the single point of failure.
mistakes.w: If a peer fails the whole peer-to-peer network stops.

mistakes.r: Both models can be used on **LANs or WANs**; the difference is the roles of devices, not size.
mistakes.w: Client-server is for WANs and P2P is for LANs.

mistakes.r: Write 'P2P is cheaper **because no server or administrator is needed**, whereas client-server needs expensive hardware and expertise'.
mistakes.w: Writing 'it is cheaper' with no comparison.

summary: You must describe how client-server networks (clients request, a central server provides and manages) and peer-to-peer networks (equal devices, each stores its own files, no server) work, give advantages and disadvantages of each, and choose and justify the right model for a scenario. It matters because it is a standard compare/recommend question on Paper 1 and links to security, hosting and the cloud.

terms.d: A device, or program such as a web browser, that sends requests to a server for a service or resource.
A powerful computer that provides services and resources to client devices and manages the network.
A network in which clients make requests to a central server that provides resources and manages the network.
A network in which all devices have equal status, each stores its own files and shares directly, with no central server.
A device on a peer-to-peer network that can act as both client and server.
A message from a client asking a server for a service or resource.
The data or service sent back from the server to the client that made the request.
A server that stores users' files centrally so they can be accessed and backed up from one place.
A server that stores web pages and sends them to browsers when requested.
A part of a system that, if it fails, causes the whole system to stop working (for example a central server).
Controlled and stored in one place, as with a server managing the files and users of a network.
Not controlled from one place; control and storage are spread across many devices, as in P2P.
A point where too much demand slows the whole system, such as an overloaded server.
Checking a user's identity, usually with a username and password, before allowing access.
A copy of data stored separately so that it can be recovered if the original is lost or damaged.
Able to grow by adding more users or resources without major redesign.

worked.ans: In a client-server network the clients send requests to a central server, which provides the files, services and security and responds to the requests, whereas in a peer-to-peer network there is no server and each computer is equal and acts as both client and server. In client-server the files are stored centrally on the server and backed up from there, but in peer-to-peer each device stores its own files and shares them directly. A client-server network is managed centrally by a network manager who sets passwords and permissions, whereas a peer-to-peer network has no central control. Client-server is more expensive because it needs a server and expertise, whereas peer-to-peer is cheaper.
worked.q: Describe the difference between a client-server network and a peer-to-peer network. [4 marks]
steps: Say what the roles are in each model.
Mention a consequence (cost, security or failure).

worked.ans: The company should use a client-server network. With 150 employees it needs to manage lots of users, and a network manager can create user accounts and passwords and update software from one place, which is much easier than looking after 150 separate computers. The records are confidential, so the server can set access permissions so only authorised staff can open customer files, and it can have a central firewall and antivirus, giving much better security than peer-to-peer where each computer is responsible for its own security. All the data is stored on the server, so it can be backed up automatically every night to another location, so that the records are not lost if a computer fails. The network can also be expanded by adding more clients or upgrading the server. A disadvantage is that it costs more and, if the server fails, staff cannot get to the records, but this can be reduced by using a backup server. Overall, client-server is the better choice because of the number of users and the sensitive data.
worked.q: A company with 150 employees stores confidential customer records. Recommend the type of network they should use. Justify your answer. [6 marks]
steps: Reason 1: many users so central management.
Reason 2: confidential data needs central security and permissions.
Reason 4: scalable, and a reliable server.
Mention the drawback (cost, single point of failure) and how to reduce it.

worked.ans: With peer-to-peer file sharing the file is available from many peers (1) so pieces can be downloaded from several peers at the same time, using the bandwidth of all of them (1). From a single server, the server's bandwidth is shared between all the clients that are downloading, so it can become overloaded and slow (1).
worked.q: Explain why downloading a popular file using peer-to-peer file sharing can be quicker than downloading it from a single server. [3 marks]
steps: In P2P the file is split into pieces held by many peers.
The client downloads different pieces from different peers at the same time.
A single server's bandwidth is shared between all clients and can be overloaded.
